segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jasper Lund's homestead stood an hour east of Earlmere, on slopes that were mostly stumps and whip-thin saplings. His drying shed had no door, only a grain sack hung on a nail. Elin Hargrove went in ahead of Garret with the lantern held high.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The racks were full. Forty cords of leaf at least, hung stem upward, every centre vein bright as a new coin from the knot down to the tip.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: They're all perfect. Every single one.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Nothing in this wood is all of anything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Elin took a leaf between finger and thumb and turned it toward the light, the way he had taught her in the mill shed. Then she rubbed, which he had not taught her at all. She held her thumb out flat.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: It came off on me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Garret pulled his gauntlet off with his teeth and took the leaf. He scraped it once with a thumbnail, held the scraping under his nose, and said nothing for long enough that Elin heard the saplings moving outside.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Whortle-berry and ash water. The fullers grey wool with it. Under the paint this vein stops a third of the way down and goes the colour of a dead moth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sack across the doorway lifted. Jasper Lund stood in it with a bucket in his hand, and he did not pretend to be surprised to see them.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: The brush is in the crock by the step. You'll want that too.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: How long?

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: Since the second week of the month.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He set the bucket down and stayed where he was.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: There isn't a tree old enough to cut between this fence and the river. My grandfather took them, then my father, then me. I walk four hours out and I come back with nine good leaves and a sore back.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Then you bring Mabel nine.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: Nine doesn't pay a carter. The draught for my mother comes up from Tollgate every ten days and the man wants coin in his hand at the door. Not fish. Not favours. Coin, on the step, or he keeps walking.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: People hang these on a saddle and ride into the Marches with them.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: I know what they hang them on.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He looked at the racks rather than at either of them.

segments.speaker: Jasper Lund
segments.text: I told myself the bad hollows are marked on every map a trader carries.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Dessa Fenwick's mule dragged her back up a slope by her own reins. She came to us to be told it was her fault. I'd have you say that to her face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The sky had gone grey over the stumps before anybody spoke about what to do. Then a man from the holding below came up the track at a run, hatless, and had to stand with his hands on his knees before he could get it out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mabel's cart had not waited for first light. It had gone at the turn of the night, because word came that Kettering's buyer caravan was at the ford and would not hold past morning. Jasper's bundles were loaded at the back with the rest.

segments.speaker: Elin Hargrove
segments.text: How far ahead is that?

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: By the time we have horses under us, a full day. And the buyer pays on sight.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was already walking for the gate.

segments.speaker: Garret Marsh
segments.text: Fetch your father's horse and fetch the trader. She knows that road better than the fool driving it.
